extracted.intended_audience: educated general readership, writers, actors, and theatre-goers interested in taste, satire, and public behaviour
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for writing satire and judging theatrical representation and comic behaviour in early-18th-century essays; addresses what makes satire vicious or virtuous, how stage-madness and acting should be handled, and social remedies for impudence and envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: avoid ill-natured personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Lampoons and Satyrs, that are written with Wit and Spirit, are like poison'd Darts, which not only inflict a Wound, but make it incurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use humour or ridicule as secret stabs to a private person's reputation. It is base and inhuman to employ wit to stir up sorrow, expose families to derision, or make virtuous people the objects of buffoonry. Talents of ridicule in the possession of ill-nature are especially dangerous; satire ought not to be anonymously aimed at the innocent or praise-worthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical taste: plays should picture human life and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: There is very little which concerns human Life, or is a Picture of Nature, that is regarded by the greater Part of the Company. The Understanding is dismissed from our Entertainments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good drama should represent human life and nature; improbable, monstrous, or incoherent spectacles that excite the laughter of fools or the wonder of idiots are signs of false taste. Evaluate plays by their fidelity to human experience, coherence, and the degree to which they engage the audience's understanding rather than mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of madness: make it humane and motivated
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes of Madness ... in Shakespear; but then it is the Disturbance of a noble Mind, from generous and humane Resentments: ... It is like that Grief which we have for the decease of our Friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing madness on stage, it should arise from a humane, noble motive (e.g., grief, noble passion) rather than being reduced to base appetites or mere grotesque behaviour. Avoid portraying 'madness' as simple appetite (e.g., thirst) or buffoonery; such depictions are inhuman and false to character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting requires understanding and truthful passion
rubrics_metrics.description: It certainly requires a Degree of Understanding to play justly; but such is our Condition, that we are to suspend our Reason to perform our Parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good acting depends on an actor's understanding of the passion and reason behind the part. Performances that devolve into physical gimmicks, appetites, or incoherent gestures (e.g., a 'madman' represented merely by 'thirst') fail the standard of humane portrayal. Critics and audiences should value truthful, reasoned embodiment of passion over mere motion or noisy effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of impudence in comedy: natural ignorance can be comic; conscious impudence is intolerable
rubrics_metrics.description: A true and genuine Impudence is ever the Effect of Ignorance, without the least Sense of it. ... No Man shall be allowed the Advantages of Impudence, who is conscious that he is such: If he knows he is impudent, he may as well be otherwise; and it shall be expected that he blush, when he sees he makes another do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impudence arising from honest ignorance may be funny and forgivable; performers or characters who are unintentionally impudent can be comic. By contrast, deliberate, self-conscious impudence (putting on an 'impudent face' as an affectation) is unacceptable and should be criticized; affectation removes the comedic virtue and makes wit detestable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting public impudence (the 'Starer'): confront and defend the offended
rubrics_metrics.description: I have given him Directions, according to the most exact Rules of Opticks, to place himself in such a Manner that he shall meet his Eyes wherever he throws them: I have Hopes that when WILL. confronts him, ... he will have some Shame, and feel a little of the Pain he has so often put others to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remedy for impudent stareers: direct confrontation (matched stares), placement to meet the offender's gaze, and male defenders taking the part of those exposed (e.g., women in church). The essay recommends active social correction rather than mere remonstration when impudence violates sacred or public spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating envy by self-deprecation and managed self-presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon hearing in a Coffee-house one of my Papers commended, I immediately apprehended the Envy that would spring from that Applause; and therefore gave a Description of my Face the next Day; being resolved as I grow in Reputation for Wit, to resign my Pretensions to Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reduce the malign effects of envy in readers, the writer counsels strategic self-deprecation or revealing unflattering personal detail. Periodic modesty or 'being dull' can console envious minds and prevent malignant responses to success; manage public persona to avoid provoking destructive envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parody/advertisement and topical irony as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: ADVERTISEMENT. For the Good of the Publick. Within two Doors of the Masquerade lives an eminent Italian Chirurgeon ... The Doctor draws Teeth without pulling off your Mask.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodying public notices and using topical, situational irony (e.g., an Italian surgeon treating masqueraders who keep their masks on) are effective satirical devices. Such mock-advertisements expose social foibles (masquerade culture, professional charlatanism) and can be used to lampoon manners and customs without necessarily attacking private reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of theatrical organisation and promotion: merit often misplaced
rubrics_metrics.description: This is to let you understand, that the Play-House is a Representation of the World in nothing so much as in this Particular, That no one rises in it according to his Merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating theatre as an institution, recognise that promotion and casting often reward spectacle, physical advantage, or novelty rather than merit. Critics should fault the system that elevates inanimate or peripheral performers and call for standards that favour genuine ability and appropriate casting, while audiences should judge productions by coherence and truthful representation rather than mere novelty.
